papers.title: Provable circuit-level thresholds for non-abelian topological phases
papers.abstract: We provide an explicit scheme to realize a quantum memory in any 2D non-chiral topological order. For this, we construct syndrome extraction circuits based on the Turaev-Viro path integral as well as a classical algorithm for decoding on the fly. We prove that our scheme has a threshold under a local stochastic circuit-level noise model and discuss how to generalize it to implement topological logical gates.

papers.title: Quantum Knowledge Distillation: State-of-the-art, Applications and Open Problems
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation transfers predictions, representations, or other supervisory information between learning models and is increasingly investigated in quantum machine learning. Its applications extend beyond compression to cross-architecture transfer, circuit approximation, distributed learning, and classical deployment of models trained using quantum-derived supervision. This survey reviews these approaches using two complementary classification axes: teacher-student configuration and the role of quantum resources in the distillation process. Quantum-inspired methods are discussed separately from methods that simulate quantum computations classically or execute them on quantum hardware. We explain how measurement probabilities, expectation values, classical readouts, state overlaps, and circuit-level objectives support different transfer mechanisms. We then critically assess the presented results against baseline design, execution conditions, uncertainty, and resource costs. The evidence shows that distillation can improve selected quantum students, but benefits are task- and architecture-dependent, and several studies find negligible gains or even performance degradation. Evaluations on physical quantum hardware remain limited, with some testing individual quantum components rather than complete learning pipelines. Heterogeneous protocols and incomplete resource reporting prevent general conclusions about practical quantum advantage. We identify priorities for controlled benchmarking, noise-aware learning, reproducible evaluation, and efficient transfer between quantum and classical models.

papers.title: Room-Temperature Quantum Emission from Boron Nitride Nanotubes
papers.abstract: Quantum information systems such as quantum key distribution and quantum communications require bright, high-purity, stable sources of single photons to act as carriers of quantum information. As such, methods for obtaining single photon emitters (SPEs) in solid-state devices capable of articulating with quantum photonic circuits are a necessary obstacle that must be overcome. Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) flakes have been extensively studied as a host material for SPEs, though working in two dimensions is accompanied by engineering complexity. However, dimensionality can be reduced through the implementation of boron nitride nanotubes (BNNTs). Here we investigate the potential of BNNTs as room-temperature SPEs using confocal photoluminescence microscopy and Hanbury Brown-Twiss interferometry. Quantum emitters were found in BNNTs spanning the entirety of the visible spectrum, including spectral regions where SPEs within hBN have not been reported. Furthermore, each tube was found to possess multiple SPEs at varying emission wavelengths along the length, exhibiting lifetimes as fast as 0.5 ns, which is about two-fold faster than the fastest hBN SPEs. Additionally, we demonstrate that surface passivation/coating mitigates blinking events, therefore increasing the emitter stability. Thus, BNNTs can function as a single structure supporting a variety of multiwavelength SPE sources, while maintaining a compact radius of ~25 nm, making them ideally suited for deterministic placement and integration within nanophotonic devices such as waveguides and interferometric filters.

papers.title: Dynamical effects induced by synthetic SU(1,1) gauge fields
papers.abstract: Compact gauge fields are powerful tools for controlling quantum dynamics and topological phases of matter. Non-compact gauge fields are particularly relevant for open systems, where particles or energy are exchanged with the environment. Here, we investigate the wavepacket and entanglement dynamics induced by an $\mathrm{SU}(1,1)$ gauge field. The wavepacket undergoes non-Abelian non-compact Bloch oscillations, in which the spectrum of an auxiliary one-dimensional quantum problem determines the transition between stable oscillations and unstable amplification. In the unstable adiabatic regime, the wavepacket probes an $\mathrm{SU}(1,1)$ topological defect, and its amplification is determined solely by a hyperbolic solid angle in Minkowski space. Threading an $\mathrm{SU}(1,1)$ gauge field through a bosonic tight-binding model yields the bosonic Kitaev model, whose volume or super-volume entanglement scaling is governed by the stability of the gauge field. We further propose an experimental realization of an $\mathrm{SU}(1,1)$ gauge field in a spinor condensate. Our results can be generalized to other non-compact groups and higher dimensions, providing a geometric framework for entanglement control, selective amplification, and engineering energy transfer.

papers.title: Polynomial-time classical simulation of boson and fermion sampling under thermal loss
papers.abstract: Sampling experiments are a leading approach to demonstrating quantum computational advantage, yet their robustness to experimental noise is not completely understood. We develop a common framework for classical simulation of boson and fermion sampling under thermal loss, including pure loss. For Fock-state boson sampling, Gaussian boson sampling with fixed uniform squeezing, and fermion sampling with magic inputs, we obtain polynomial-time sampling at inverse-polynomial total variation error, for any fixed nonzero overall loss rate, and with high probability over Haar-random interferometers. A milder flatness assumption on the ideal output distribution suffices for quasipolynomial-time simulation without Haar randomness. With constant thermal loss per layer, the same flatness assumption gives polynomial-time simulation at logarithmic depth. Our bounds for Fock-state boson sampling cover both dilute and saturated regimes and become stronger near full input filling: when only a bounded number of input modes are empty, the noisy output for Haar-random interferometers converges, as the number of modes grows, to a distribution independent of the interferometer.

papers.title: DiffSequence-Q: Diffusion Design with Quantum Assistance for Biologically Active Proteins
papers.abstract: Designing protein sequences that satisfy both secondary structure requirements and solubility targets remains challenging. We present DiffSequence-Q, a hybrid multinomial diffusion model conditioned on secondary structure at each residue and a continuous solubility target. To introduce quantum auxiliary supervision during training, we employ a quantum neural network (QNN) or quantum Kolmogorov-Arnold network (QKAN) as an auxiliary solubility prediction head over shared Transformer representations. The auxiliary prediction loss is jointly optimized with the diffusion objective, allowing quantum auxiliary supervision to influence the learned denoising model. Once trained, protein sequences are generated entirely through classical reverse diffusion. On the CATH benchmark, DiffSequence-Q achieved the highest secondary structure recovery among the four evaluated models for complete sequence generation. Evaluation with a separately trained solubility prediction model showed that the best QNN and QKAN configurations achieved mean predicted solubility scores 14.0% and 22.7% higher than the multilayer perceptron (MLP) baseline, respectively. Experimental characterization further demonstrated biological activity across three distinct protein families. Selected defensins exhibited pronounced inhibitory activity against Aspergillus niger, while xylanases and short-chain dehydrogenases exhibited substantial enzymatic activity. Together, these results support DiffSequence-Q as a framework for integrating structural requirements and solubility targets in protein generation, with experimentally demonstrated biological activity.

papers.title: Quantum enhanced beam displacement estimation: sensitivity limits, optimal probes, and measurement schemes
papers.abstract: We investigate the ultimate sensitivity limits for measuring small transverse beam displacements and identify optimal strategies that attain them, using the framework of mode parameter estimation. We contrast two families of states with different resource constraints, using Hermite-Gauss and Laguerre-Gauss mode pairs. First, for fixed total photon number states, the optimal state is identified and we show that it asymptotically approaches a rotated NOON state. The sensitivity bound is compared to that of an asymptotically optimal pure Gaussian state with fixed average photon number. Finally, we propose concrete measurement schemes using the method of moments and show that the twin-Fock state may provide a viable alternative to the rotated NOON state for this task. Our work provides a broader benchmark for developing practical strategies for spatial sensing at the quantum limit.

papers.title: Disorder-blind Mpemba acceleration of quantum state preparation
papers.abstract: Using the strong Mpemba effect to accelerate relaxation by initial-state design requires suppressing the slowest mode, which typically needs prior knowledge of the system. However, in disordered systems, this mode is sample-dependent, so a fixed preparation generally retains a slow-mode overlap. We show that a ``blind'' preparation, designed from the clean chain without knowledge of the disorder realisation or its distribution, can start farther from stationarity yet overtake a reference in typical samples of a dephased disordered XX chain. It requires only the chain geometry and the particle number. At strong dephasing, the density dynamics maps to a resistor chain, and an exact inverse-generator identity links the residual overlap to the spatial resistance profile. We find two distinct thresholds: a finite mean resistance suffices for diffusion, but the residual overlap decays as $L^{-1/2}$ with chain length $L$ only when the resistance variance is finite; rare weak links slow this decay. We predict the fraction of samples in which the blind preparation wins, which is an ensemble-level measure of its reliability. Finite-size calculations support both scaling regimes with interactions at strong dephasing. We give preparation circuits and a density readout for the residual overlap.

papers.title: Recalibration-Aware Optimization of ZEFOZ Operating Points in $^{167}\mathrm{Er}^{3+}:\mathrm{Y}_2\mathrm{SiO}_5$ for Quantum Memories
papers.abstract: Erbium-doped solids like $^{167}\mathrm{Er}^{3+}:\mathrm{Y}_2\mathrm{SiO}_5$ have properties that make them suitable for quantum-network memories, however, their unquenched effective electronic spin causes rapid magnetic decoherence. Operating at Zero First-Order Zeeman (ZEFOZ) points allows us to mitigate this, where we evaluate the ZEFOZ landscape for Site-2 $^{167}\mathrm{Er}^{3+}$ by incorporating a full-Hessian spin-Hamiltonian treatment with the anisotropic magnetic-field covariance derived from the native $^{89}\mathrm{Y}$ crystal lattice directly. Operating-point screening criteria were adopted to devise a Pareto-optimal frontier of four transition pairs to balance modeled Y-only magnetic pure-dephasing lifetimes ($T_{φ,Y}^{(2)}$) against microwave control authority. The $ε_{14}\leftrightarrowε_{15}$ transition exhibits the longest modeled Y-bath-induced quadratic pure-dephasing time, $T_{φ,Y}^{(2)}>2.2\times10^5~\mathrm{s}$, while the $ε_{12}\leftrightarrowε_{13}$ transition stood out, achieving a Rabi frequency coefficient of $1.248 \times 10^5~\mathrm{Hz/mT}$. An assumption-based Hamiltonian-uncertainty analysis demonstrates that while uncompensated deviations shift the ZEFOZ condition away from its nominal magnetic-field coordinate, the shifted operating points can be recovered via numerical vector-field recalibration. The Pareto-optimal coordinates were mathematically recovered for all sampled Hamiltonian perturbations, and the $84.1^{\mathrm{st}}$-percentile field relocations ranged from $10.95$ to $27.97~\mathrm{mT}$. The intended operation near $10~\mathrm{mK}$ must be taken into account for the suppression of Er-induced spectral diffusion through electronic-spin polarization, while the extended Y-bath pure-dephasing timescales also remain conditional on the adopted temporal-correlation model.

papers.title: Asymptotic analysis of the dynamical field-field correlation function of the impenetrable Bose gas
papers.abstract: We study the long-time, large-distance asymptotic behaviour of the two-point correlation function of fields of the impenetrable Bose gas in equilibrium states characterized by a quasi-momentum distribution (or filling fraction). This includes, in particular, the cases of Gibbs and generalized Gibbs ensembles. The overall structure of the asymptotic expansion depends on the number of Fermi points, those points for which the quasi-momentum distribution takes the value $1/2$. The leading asymptotic behaviour is determined by a relaxation rate, a logarithmic correction term and an amplitude for which we provide simple and explicit expressions. In the case of two Fermi points the first sub-leading correction is calculated as well.

papers.title: Atomic Static Electric Quadrupole Polarizability from Relativistic Many-Body Theory With Application To Thulium $\left(6s^2\, 4f^{13}\right)$\, $^2F_{7/2}$ and $^2F_{5/2}$
papers.abstract: In the present work a method for calculating atomic static electric rank-$n$ tensor quadrupole polarizabilities $α_Q^{(n)}(J)$ for arbitrary atomic electronic structure is presented. It is based on a linear-symmetry representation of atomic states using large-scale relativistic configuration interaction wavefunctions, and the quadrupole polarizabilities are obtained by a sum-over-states approach. The major result from applying this method to atomic thulium is $α_Q^{(0)}(\frac{7}{2}) = 2496^{+0}_{-231}$ \au for the electronic ground term $^2F_{7/2}$ static electric scalar quadrupole polarizability which is roughly a factor of four smaller than same property in the electronic ground state of the cesium atom. This finding adds to the favorable properties of thulium atoms in atomic-clock research.

papers.title: Testing Gravitationally-Induced-Entanglement with Massive Particles and Quantum Clocks
papers.abstract: We present an experimental proposal to test whether gravity can entangle a levitated particle with an array of quantum clocks. By harnessing the collective interaction between a micrometer-scale particle and an array of ultra-precise nuclear clocks, our scheme offers a conceivable path to observing gravitationally mediated entanglement with quantum clocks in the laboratory. Crucially, this setup will probe a genuinely relativistic effect one that requires the contribution of internal clock energy to active gravitational mass and cannot arise from the Newtonian interaction between fixed masses. Therefore, observing this entanglement would provide evidence for the quantised nature of active gravitational mass -- which has not been tested in any prior experiment -- rather than for spatial coherence of fixed masses,which is routinely tested in matterwave interferometers

papers.title: Recovery gates as a resource in repetition-code process tomography: exhaustive gate-optimal designs for three, five and seven qubits
papers.abstract: Process tomography built on stabilizer codes compares the logical channel of a repetition code with a reference channel, and the decoder that produces that channel is almost always fixed to the standard minimum-weight one. We ask how many physical single-qubit Pauli gates the decoder actually needs when the measurement basis is fixed---the constraint under which the count is a resource rather than a bookkeeping artefact. Exhaustive enumeration of every recovery design for $n=3$, $5$ and $7$ qubits, with rank decided by exact modular arithmetic at two primes, gives minimal counts of $0$, $1$ and $5$ gates, against $6$, $10$ and $14$ for first-order decoding and $6$, $50$ and $308$ for full minimum-weight decoding. The count depends only on how many sites are corrected and never on which, so the two halves of the design problem separate. Correcting more sites is not monotonically better: at $n=7$ full decoding loses three dimensions of rank, and under a calibration-residual floor the precision curve at $n=3$ is U-shaped. The three-gate design is $9.5$ times more precise than the standard six-gate decoder at the median of $40$ sampled working points, and more precise at every one of them ($1.8$ to $88$ times); the size of that factor belongs to the working point, the ordering does not. Reaching a $10$\,mrad rms error then costs $1.2\times10^{7}$ shots in $65$\,s on a current superconducting device at a well-conditioned point, while $n\ge5$ stays out of reach for conditioning reasons rather than gate-count reasons. Finally, the optimal designs are not covariant under chain reversal: they separate the mirror pair of arXiv:2610.19779 by $1.3\times10^{-3}$ while leaving the Jacobian at full rank.

papers.title: Beyond Quantum Messages: Toward Quantum-Native Network Functioning
papers.abstract: The Quantum Internet is commonly envisioned as a network that transports quantum states and distributes entanglement as the key resource underpinning distributed quantum applications. This view is necessary but incomplete if quantum phenomena are confined to what the network carries or manages, while network functionalities remain grounded predominantly in classical abstractions. This Perspective advances a broader thesis: quantum phenomena can also participate directly in the realization of network functionalities. We first establish the architectural baseline by introducing entanglement as a stateful network resource whose operational condition is non-locally distributed across remote nodes, evolves through manipulation or consumption, and degrades over time through decoherence. Its evolving state must therefore remain visible to the functionalities acting on it. We then move beyond resource visibility and use two mechanisms as proof points of a broader quantum-native functional design space: entanglement generation during propagation through coherent spatial-path superposition, and operational connectivity induced by shared entanglement that can depart from the physical graph. These examples show that paths, neighbors, or participating nodes may become operationally relevant in ways determined by quantum coherence and shared entanglement, rather than by physical connectivity alone. We identify Quantum Addressing as a transversal abstraction capable of representing such relations while complementing, rather than replacing, classical addressing and signaling. The resulting perspective broadens the Quantum Internet from transporting quantum information and distributing entanglement to exploiting quantum phenomena in network functioning, opening a coupled frontier spanning routing, forwarding, control, and functionality placement.

papers.title: Dualities in one-dimensional quantum lattice models: Lie groups, Schur-Weyl duality and symmetry breaking
papers.abstract: We present a systematic framework for gauging continuous symmetries, and show that the Schur-Weyl duality arises naturally as a realization of this construction with open boundary conditions. Restricting to compact Lie group symmetries, we construct dual models for one-dimensional quantum lattice models exhibiting those symmetries. We demonstrate that matrix product operators enable the explicit construction of intertwiners between the dual theories and their (non-invertible) symmetries. With closed boundary conditions, we can relate the full spectrum of these dual theories by considering all possible twisted boundary conditions.We illustrate how the Peter-Weyl transform appears when the duality acts on the boundary Hilbert space of a $G$-symmetric model. The presented framework generalizes previous work on dualities for unitary fusion category symmetric models. It exemplifies how dualities for both finite and continuous symmetries rely on the relation between a bond algebra and a representation of the symmetry in the lattice as double centralizers. We argue that dual non-invertible spontaneous symmetry breaking is the mechanism that underlies symmetric tensor network algorithms. We illustrate these results for $U(1)$- and $SU(2)$-symmetric quantum lattice models.

papers.title: Entropic measures of quantum information
papers.abstract: Entropy has played a pivotal role in physics ever since its inception by Clausius in the early industrial age. Shannon ushered the concept into the information age by using it to describe fundamental limits of information processing, founding the field of information theory. Today, a fruitful interaction between information theory and physics is pushing our understanding of entropy forward. It has revealed, in particular, that no single notion of entropy suffices to capture all relevant properties of physical systems, making it necessary to consider a variety of entropic measures of quantum information, each with distinct features and uses. This review surveys these recent advances in a structured way, covering a comprehensive array of information measures, including Rényi and smooth entropies, together with their interrelations. Starting with a systematic characterization of entropies that motivates their definitions from natural physical principles, we discuss their applications ranging from quantum communication and cryptography to resource theories, thermodynamics, and many-body physics.

papers.title: Certifying quantum code and circuit distances at scale
papers.abstract: Code and circuit distances characterize how strongly quantum error correction suppresses logical errors and guide code comparisons, schedule choices and resource estimates. Yet many published distances are only upper bounds from heuristic searches. Here, we express both distances as tropical partition functions and evaluate them with rank-based dynamic programming and weight-bounded search. Circuit reductions and relaxations shrink the problems, and proved lower bounds with explicit logical errors of matching weight certify exact values. On two benchmarks, our method certifies more instances than all other tested exact solvers combined. We certify distances for codes with up to 31,200 qubits, such as Google's modular hyperbolic codes, and for memory circuits with up to $8\times10^5$ fault mechanisms, such as those of high-rate Cornucopia codes. Our audit of 26 recent papers identifies overestimated distances and non-tight upper bounds in 10 papers, with a maximum discrepancy of at least eight. Certified distances also guide circuit design and show which defective chips remain usable. In particular, we certify circuit distance 16 for IBM's two-gross memory circuits with the standard schedule, not the assumed 18, whereas redesigned schedules reach 18 at one noisy cycle, at the cost of one more timestep per cycle. At 99.98% junction yield, keeping gross-code memory blocks with dead checks that are certified at distance 10 or more raises the estimated usable share from 53% for perfect blocks alone to 94% with an improved schedule.

papers.title: Finite-Time Thermodynamic Routing in an Anharmonic Collective Quantum Otto Engine
papers.abstract: The Gibbs state determined by a thermal reservoir does not determine how a working medium approaches it or how fluctuations accumulate over repeated cycles. We exploit this kinetic freedom in an anharmonic collective quantum Otto engine. A longitudinal interaction separates neighboring Dicke transition frequencies without changing their collective matrix elements, allowing passive spectral shaping to route finite-time transport among edges with different heat costs while preserving the contact Gibbs states. Exact edge-current identities and repeated-cycle counting statistics link this routing to mean work, hot heat, and intercycle work correlations. At fixed thermal-contact exposure, structured reservoirs can increase both mean work and long-time squared precision; equal-work controls distinguish these gains from uniform relaxation-rate changes. The useful regime is mesoscopic, bounded by spectral resolution and physical contact time. An equal-cooling example and a full-spin local-noise study test the mechanism beyond ideal engine operation, the latter retaining a one-cycle precision gain despite spin-sector mixing. In a six-transmon dressed-spectrum model, passive microwave filters at fixed integrated coupling achieve equal mean work with shorter thermal contacts, corresponding to higher contact-time-normalized output, and with long-time squared precision comparable to that of the fastest sampled flat reference. The transition pathways selected by a passive reservoir thus provide a control variable for finite-time performance and accumulated work fluctuations that is independent of thermal equilibrium.

papers.title: Persistent level-resolved transmon population after dispersive readout, and the limits of its open-system description
papers.abstract: We calculate the level-resolved transmon population remaining after dispersive readout with a converged open-system model. The drive and qubit-cavity coupling use the rotating-wave approximation, while the cavity is a quantized mode in a frame displaced by its classical trajectory. At a readout occupation of 80, the model leaves a persistent distribution across the first transmon levels, with p2 = 1.02 x 10^-3 and p3 = 4.10 x 10^-5 at the end of readout. These populations survive an additional drive-off wait: over 73 ns each level decays by less than 3 percent and follows its own relaxation rate, not the near-factor-of-two drop in residual cavity photons. This identifies the population as bare-level occupation rather than coherent dressing. Channel-removal and bath-model controls attribute p2 mainly to dephasing and p3 and above mainly to relaxation, unchanged across bath models though absolute values vary by up to 15 percent. We also test the coherent drive truncation. In dissipation-free transmon-only benchmarks driven by the classical cavity trajectory, the nearest-neighbour RWA drive underestimates the full charge-operator result while the drive is on. At switch-off for occupation 80, where coherent populations are hundreds of times larger than the residual values, p2(RWA)/p2(full) = 0.905 and p3(RWA)/p3(full) = 0.759, with larger discrepancies at deeper levels. One source is a parity-allowed non-nearest-neighbour charge matrix element omitted by the drive operator. A naive beyond-RWA extension with bare-basis Lindblad dissipators fails a zero-drive ground-state test and serves only as a diagnostic. A dressed-basis (secular) construction instead leaves the dressed ground state stationary at zero drive. The result is a converged RWA prediction of readout-induced population plus direct tests of where the approximation loses quantitative reliability.

papers.title: Optimal finite-copy readout of three-qubit entanglement with state retention
papers.abstract: For unknown three-qubit pure states, we characterize the optimal trade-off among GHZ-class certification, binary probability readout of the three-tangle, and conditional state retention. The vanishing ideal of the null class specifies the optimal certification subspace, while a polynomial multiplication operator gives the spectral limit for binary readout. Four copies are necessary for a nonzero certificate. A fifth copy raises the optimal success probability from $τ^{2}/48$ to $5τ^{2}/72$ and permits the original unknown state to be retained, where $τ$ is the three-tangle. We obtain this gain as an instance of a general symmetry-based additional-copy theorem. At six copies the optimal certification probability is $(39+2S)τ^{2}/296$, with $S=\sum_{X}\mathrm{Tr}\,ρ_{X}^{2}$, whereas the largest exact binary probability is $τ^{2}/8$. Local Schur measurements and conditional local operations with classical communication attain these bounds. Retaining the full six-copy branch record yields a weighted estimator with lower variance than binary thinning of the same data. Explicit circuits and fixed-budget comparisons connect the success probabilities to input-copy consumption, retained quantum output, and coherent gate cost.

papers.title: QDiff: Differential Testing of Quantum Software Stacks
papers.abstract: Over the past few years, several quantum software stacks (QSS) have been developed in response to rapid hardware advances in quantum computing. A QSS includes a quantum programming language, an optimizing compiler that translates a quantum algorithm written in a high-level language into quantum gate instructions, a quantum simulator that emulates these instructions on a classical device, and a software controller that sends analog signals to a very expensive quantum hardware based on quantum circuits. In comparison to traditional compilers and architecture simulators, QSSes are difficult to tests due to the probabilistic nature of results, the lack of clear hardware specifications, and quantum programming complexity. This work devises a novel differential testing approach for QSSes, named QDIFF with three major innovations: (1) We generate input programs to be tested via semantics-preserving, source to source transformation to explore program variants. (2) We speed up differential testing by filtering out quantum circuits that are not worthwhile to execute on quantum hardware by analyzing static characteristics such as a circuit depth, 2 qubit gate operations, gate error rates, and T1 relaxation time. (3) We design an extensible equivalence checking mechanism via distribution comparison functions such as Kolmogorov Smirnov test and cross entropy

papers.title: Quantum Fourier integration of decay rates at next-to-leading order
papers.abstract: We discuss the use of quantum neural networks (QNNs) as a tool for integrating decay rates at next-to-leading order (NLO) in perturbation theory. Data-encoding quantum circuits admit a truncated Fourier-series representation, enabling a trained QNN to approximate a target integrand and provide the coefficients subsequently integrated with Quantum Fourier Iterative Amplitude Estimation (QFIAE). The causal-unitary formulation of the Loop-Tree Duality (LTD) combines virtual and real contributions into locally finite integrands suitable for this representation. We consider $H\to q\bar q(g)$, $γ^*\to q\bar q(g)$ and $Φ\toφφ(φ)$, comparing quantum-simulator and quantum-hardware results with analytic NLO predictions. The study illustrates the potential of Fourier-based QNN integration for high-energy physics.

papers.title: Quantum Advantage with Sign-Free Proofs: An Oracle Separation between $\mathsf{StoqMA}$ and $\mathsf{MA}$
papers.abstract: Several landmark oracle results (FOCS 2000, FOCS 2025, STOC 2026) establish strict separations along the chain $\mathsf{MA} \subseteq \mathsf{QCMA} \subseteq \mathsf{QMA}$, showing that quantum verification and quantum witnesses can each provide additional power over classical proof systems. These separations, however, use substantial coherent quantum computation, often through the quantum Fourier transform. We prove that a minimal quantum resource already suffices to outperform every classical verifier. Namely, we show the separation $$\mathsf{MA} \subsetneq \mathsf{StoqMA}$$ relative to a classical oracle. The class $\mathsf{StoqMA}$, introduced by Bravyi, Bessen, and Terhal (arXiv 2006), restricts the verifier to classical reversible computation, followed by a single Hadamard-basis measurement. Its power is closely tied to the complexity of stoquastic Hamiltonians, a sign-problem-free and seemingly more tractable class of quantum Hamiltonians. Our separating problem is to determine whether a sparse high-girth graph, given via an adjacency-list oracle, has a large or small Perron--Frobenius eigenvalue. This amounts to a ground-energy estimation task for a related stoquastic Hamiltonian. Our construction builds on a line of work on graph exploration problems with exponential quantum speedups, from welded trees (STOC 2003) to recent constructions (STOC 2021, arXiv 2026).

papers.title: Coherent phase slips in coupled rings: from weak to strong interactions
papers.abstract: We study the coherent transfer of circulation between two weakly coupled lattice rings of ultracold bosons, in which a persistent current initially prepared in one ring oscillates back and forth between the rings without net transfer of particles. Combining Bose--Hubbard simulations with their Gross--Pitaevskii and quantum phase model limits, we show that similar current oscillations arise from two distinct microscopic mechanisms. At weak interactions, particles in each occupied momentum mode tunnel independently between the rings, leading to a transfer time inversely proportional to the inter-ring tunnelling, extensive particle-number fluctuations and entanglement distributed over many Schmidt components; this mode-exchange dynamics is suppressed by self-trapping as the interactions increase. At stronger interactions and large filling, in the phase-dominated regime, circulation is instead transferred through a second-order collective process between many-body persistent-current states, with a transfer time scaling as the inverse square of the inter-ring tunnelling in the weak-link limit. Number fluctuations then remain of order one instead of growing with the particle number, and within each number sector the system evolves into coherent superpositions of two many-body configurations, distinguished by which ring carries the circulation. The entanglement accessible under number-conserving operations therefore reaches up to approximately one bit. We propose a quench protocol to prepare the initial state and estimate transfer times within reach of current ring-lattice experiments, identifying coupled rings as a platform to study coherent quantum phase slips and to manipulate persistent-current states.

papers.title: Primitive Quantum Gates for an $SU(3)$ Discrete Subgroup: $Σ(216\times3)$
papers.abstract: We construct a primitive gate set for the digital quantum simulation of the $648$-element discrete subgroup of $SU(3)$, $\dsb$. The five algorithmic primitives are the inversion, group multiplication, trace, group Fourier transform, and kinetic-phase gates, for which we provide qubit and qutrit--qubit decompositions. For a fiducial shear-viscosity calculation on a $10^3$ spatial lattice with $50$ time steps and a total synthesis-error budget of $10^{-8}$, the estimated fault-tolerant costs are $2.3$--$6.8\times10^{10}$ $T$ gates in the qubit architecture and $1.3$--$5.9\times10^{12}$ $R$ gates in the qutrit--qubit architecture.

papers.title: Non-Unitary Quantum Butterfly Effect: Theory and Experiment
papers.abstract: We present a generalization of the out of time order correlator (OTOC) for non-unitary systems. For a Haar-random brickwork qudit-circuit, peppered with local, projective measurement, we calculate the infinite-temperature, ensemble-average OTOC. Utilizing transfer matrix machinery, we find that the OTOC asymptotically decays exponentially and that the decay depends on the rate of measurement. In the thermodynamic limit, with sparse measurement, the OTOC approximately exhibits a Gaussian shape. Phenomenologically, this corresponds to the development of a causal scrambling front where unlike the unitary case, the signal decays in the bulk of the causal cone. We develop a Monte Carlo framework to compute the OTOC. We then estimate the OTOC directly via quantum simulation and on Quantinuum's trapped-ion quantum computer. We resolve the unitary and non-unitary OTOC phenomenology despite the presence of hardware noise. Our analytic results characterize how local nonunitary channels affect OTOC decay, providing a quantitative benchmark for the cumulative effects of a broad class of hardware noise on many-body dynamics.

papers.title: Machine learning quantum data to accelerate quantum Monte Carlo
papers.abstract: Simulating strongly correlated electrons in molecules and materials remains a central goal for quantum computing. A promising strategy uses quantum processors to prepare trial wavefunctions that guide classical quantum Monte Carlo (QMC). However, the enormous computational cost of repeatedly processing quantum measurements has severely limited the practical scalability of this approach. Here, we overcome this bottleneck by compressing quantum measurement data into machine-learning models that efficiently provide the wavefunction overlaps needed by QMC. This accelerates quantum-classical QMC by orders of magnitude, enabling chemically accurate simulations on up to 40 qubits, more than doubling the scale of previous hardware demonstrations with comparable accuracy. We demonstrate our approach on hydrogen chains and strongly correlated iron-sulfur clusters using measurements from Google's Willow processor. By enabling efficient reuse of quantum-state information on the classical coprocessor, our framework addresses a fundamental bottleneck in hybrid quantum algorithms that will persist even into the fault-tolerant era.

papers.title: Accelerating Quantum-Classical Auxiliary-Field Quantum Monte Carlo with Shadow-Trained Neural Quantum States
papers.abstract: Quantum-classical auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (QC-AFQMC) uses a trial state prepared on a quantum computer to improve the accuracy of the classical AFQMC algorithm. State-of-the-art QC-AFQMC represents this state with matchgate shadows, so every trial-walker overlap and local energy must be averaged over many snapshots, making this classical computation a bottleneck. Here we distill the matchgate shadow data into a symmetry-constrained, noise-aware, autoregressive transformer neural quantum state (NQS). Used as the AFQMC trial state, the NQS evaluates overlaps, force biases, and local energies without repeatedly summing over the matchgate shadows. For a nickel-catalyzed oxidative-addition reaction, the noise-awareness of our NQS design successfully recovers the ideal-upCCD AFQMC barrier and reaction energy within statistical uncertainty, while standard QC-AFQMC execution with the same shadow data yields qualitatively inaccurate results as a result of hardware noise. Since the shadow data are needed only for training, the estimated classical cost for the nickel system falls by approximately 99% relative to our previous QC-AFQMC implementation.

papers.title: Semi-Analytical Geometric Synthesis of Robust Quantum Controls
papers.abstract: High-fidelity quantum gates are a central requirement for fault-tolerant quantum computation, yet their implementation is limited by the sensitivity of qubits to environmental noise and by control non-idealities. To mitigate these effects, quantum gates can be designed as dynamically corrected gates (DCGs), where control sequences are engineered to suppress the impact of errors on the resulting operation. Many methods in the literature are able to synthesize DCGs, but they typically rely on numerical optimization, with synthesis times on the order of minutes per gate. Here, we propose an automated semi-analytical method that reduces this cost by orders of magnitude, synthesizing smooth, robust control pulses in tens of milliseconds rather than minutes, with comparable fidelity and robustness. Our approach is based on the Space Curve Quantum Control (SCQC) formalism, where quantum evolution is mapped onto a geometric space curve whose geometric properties determine the target gate and its robustness. We parameterize the curve in the Frenet-Serret frame and employ the Pontryagin Maximum Principle (PMP) to design controls that are robust against both amplitude and dephasing errors. The PMP is formulated as a boundary-value problem and solved using a shooting method. The Frenet-Serret frame is integrated using Rodrigues' formula. Starting from a reference solution, we gradually vary the target rotation angle to construct a library of solutions, whose interpolation provides initial guesses for the shooting parameters of new target gates. We evaluated the method on 2,000 single-qubit rotations, obtaining a mean local optimization time of 39.945 ms per gate after preparation of the interpolation base. Quantum propagation yielded nominal gate infidelities below 10^-9 after virtual phase correction, with verified robustness against quasistatic amplitude and dephasing errors.

papers.title: Quantum trajectory of a spin oscillator, continuous retrodiction beyond the Heisenberg uncertainty relation
papers.abstract: The Heisenberg uncertainty relation in quantum mechanics limits the precision of predicting the outcome of measurements of any non-commuting observables. However, this restriction does not apply to retrodictive guessing of the outcomes of past measurements. Here, we experimentally demonstrate this using a spin oscillator consisting of $ 5.17 \times 10^{10}$ rubidium atoms. Through weak continuous measurements, we monitor canonical spin observables $\hat{x}_{\mathrm{A}}$ and $\hat{p}_{\mathrm{A}}$ with $[\hat{x}_{\mathrm{A}},\hat{p}_{\mathrm{A}}] = i\hbar$. By combining information obtained before and after time $t$, we retrodict the outcomes of measurements of $\hat{x}_{\mathrm{A}}$ and $\hat{p}_{\mathrm{A}}$ at time $t$ with variances that remain, concurrently over 1.4 hours, $\sim$ 1.01 dB below the bound set by the Heisenberg uncertainty relation. We also infer and demonstrate the ability to retrodict, with the same precision, the measurement outcomes for arbitrary quadratures of the spin oscillator. This brings interesting prospects for further research on quantum measurements, and for quantum-enhanced sensing that combines trajectory and entanglement strategies.

papers.title: Quantum Gouy phase singularities in a propagating biphoton state
papers.abstract: Phase singularities are topological defects around which the phase winds by an integer multiple of $2π$. In entangled multiphoton states, they can emerge nonlocally in the joint wavefunction rather than in the field of either subsystem alone. Here we show that the quantum Gouy phase generates nonlocal phase singularities (NPSs) in the two-dimensional longitudinal propagation space of entangled photon pairs. We consider photon pairs produced via spontaneous parametric down-conversion pumped by a Laguerre--Gaussian beam, with the signal and idler photons propagating independently over different longitudinal distances. The accumulated radial-mode-dependent Gouy phases induce destructive interference among biphoton spatial-mode components, producing isolated intensity nulls with quantized phase winding. For a pump with radial mode number $p$, the NPS topological charges have magnitude $p$, whereas their propagation positions and charge signs are governed by the Rayleigh ranges of the pump and phase-matching functions. We further identify the radial-mode structure required for their formation, showing that separable biphoton states cannot support isolated longitudinal NPSs. Our results extend nonlocal singular optics from transverse spatial correlations to longitudinal propagation dynamics and establish propagation distance as a coordinate space for topological structures in entangled photon pairs.

papers.title: The Logic of Partitions and Partition Logics: Ore's Correspondence, Contextual Pasting, and Direct-Sum Decompositions
papers.abstract: The term ``partition logic'' denotes two constructions at different levels. In automaton and generalized-urn models, selected partitions generate Boolean event algebras whose contextwise union forms a concrete pasted event structure; in Ellerman's framework, whole partitions are classifications governed by refinement and partition operations. For a finite set $U$, Ore's correspondence maps each generator $π$ to its Boolean algebra $\BA(π)$, but it neither identifies the pasted carrier with $\Part(U)$ nor makes pasting a partition operation. It yields $\BA(π\wedgeσ)=\BA(π)\cap\BA(σ)$ and $\BA(π\veeσ)=\langle\BA(π)\cup\BA(σ)\rangle_{\rm BA}$, where $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\rm BA}$ denotes Boolean-algebra generation. Thus meet captures the common event algebra, whereas join gives the ambient Boolean closure. Chinese-lantern, Firefly, and triangular examples distinguish shared events, atomic intertwining, and inherited concrete order. Ellerman's direct-sum decompositions (DSDs) provide a vector-space analogue: component projections of an orthogonal DSD resolve the identity and encode exclusive outcomes, but its components are not equivalence classes of vectors. Gleason and Kochen--Specker applications require globally context-consistent valuations on those projections.

papers.title: The Thermodynamic Cost of Computing with Heat
papers.abstract: Autonomous quantum thermal machines have recently been proposed as physics-based computing substrates where logical inputs and outputs are encoded in temperature gradients. While such ``thermodynamic neurons'' exhibit a clear trade-off between computational fidelity and heat dissipation, the fundamental information-theoretic limits of temperature-encoded computation remain uncharacterized. Here, we derive rigorous bounds linking average error probability, channel capacity, and entropy production for finite-capacity thermal reservoirs operating far from equilibrium. We prove that the minimal dissipation required to achieve a target average error probability $\langle ξ\rangle$ diverges as $\langle ξ\rangle$ approaches a fundamental minimum error floor $\epsMin$ imposed by finite-reservoir thermal fluctuations. We further establish a thermodynamic channel capacity that saturates at high dissipation, and quantify the minimal dissipation required for cascaded networks to maintain target fidelity. We demonstrate that the required dissipation grows linearly $\mathcal{O}(L)$ with network depth for shallow networks, but diverges as the network depth $L$ approaches a fundamental maximum limit $L_{\max} = \epsNet/\epsMin$ imposed by the minimum error floor. Furthermore, under strong noise amplification conditions, the required dissipation can grow up to $\mathcal{O}(L^3)$. Our framework bridges stochastic thermodynamics, finite-time information theory, and autonomous computation, providing rigorous design principles for energy-efficient analog thermodynamic hardware.

papers.title: Two-copy distillability of one-copy-undistillable negative-partial-transpose states in every dimension
papers.abstract: Whether entanglement with a negative partial transpose (NPT) can be undistillable is a longstanding open problem. In the canonical family of DiVincenzo \textit{et al.}, the one-copy-undistillable region was conjectured to remain undistillable at all copy numbers. We refute this: in every dimension $d\geq3$, one vertex of this region is two-copy distillable, via an explicit Schmidt-rank-two tight-frame witness. The separation persists on an open set, while other states in the same region are provably two-copy undistillable. Twirling our counterexample into Werner form makes it two-copy undistillable, so this standard reduction can erase finite-copy distillability.

papers.title: State preparation via measurement and feedback: pushing relations, state structures, and non-invertible symmetries
papers.abstract: Quantum circuits with measurements and unitary feedback (MF) can prepare long-range entangled states in constant depth, but a systematic construction of the MF preparation circuit for a given target state remains underexplored. We develop such a scheme for one-dimensional states, based on the notion of pushable defects: virtual-bond operators of a matrix product state that can be pushed through the tensor at the price of a physical feedback unitary. We show that the set of pushable defects, together with their pushing relations classifies finite-depth MF-preparable states and dictates their preparation circuits. To each class of the target state $|A\rangle$, we associate a state $|B\rangle$ from which $|A\rangle$ can be prepared using a 1-round MF circuit; in particular, $|A\rangle$ is preparable from a product state using a circuit with 1 round of MF whenever $|B\rangle$ is preparable by a finite-depth local unitary (FDLU) circuit. For a general target state, the scheme is obtained by iterating this procedure until the associated state is FDLU-preparable. For open-boundary matrix product states, the scheme is complete: it constructs a preparation circuit whenever finite-depth MF preparation with left-conditioned feedback corrections is possible. Pushable defects and pushing relations thus emerge as a unifying principle for quantum state preparation via measurements and feedback. This characterization further reveals an intrinsic connection between MF circuits and non-invertible symmetries: states with certain classes of pushing relations are related to a product state by Tambara-Yamagami duality operators, or by continuous cosine symmetry operators with fusion rules $L_α L_{α'} = L_{α+α'} + L_{α-α'}$, together with their generalizations up to (not necessarily transversal) gates.

papers.title: Certified Misty-State Rewriting (A Question-and-Answer Guide)
papers.abstract: Quantum mechanics is difficult to teach because its conceptual content and mathematical notation usually arrive together. Rudolph's misty-state language was designed to decouple those burdens; basis states are visual objects, clouds represent superposition, gates act by elementary replacement rules, and destructive interference appears as cancellation rather than as matrix calculation. An elementary ``misty-state'' language can make quantum circuits accessible to students before they master complex linear algebra. Development presented here was initiated/led by the first author. The contribution is not a replacement for complete graphical calculi such as ZX or sum-over-paths. It is a source-specific bridge from an intuitive educational notation to a mathematically explicit, executable, and falsifiable semantics.

papers.title: Symmetry Constraints Regularize Neural Quantum State Learning
papers.abstract: Neural quantum states (NQS) offer highly expressive variational wavefunctions, but their optimization is frequently bottlenecked by redundant parameters and poorly conditioned landscapes. We demonstrate that embedding Hamiltonian symmetries directly into the variational parameterization geometrically regularizes this learning problem. For Boltzmann-family NQS, we enforce symmetries by tying local Pauli-$Z$ generators along physical geometric orbits, analytically collapsing the trainable coefficient space prior to optimization. To quantify the resulting optimization geometry, we introduce a geometric metric built on the Jacobian and Hessian of the optimization landscape. This framework evaluates the fraction of the physically accessible state space that corresponds to high-quality, low-energy solutions. Evaluating our approach on transverse-field Ising (TFIM) and XXZ spin chains shows that symmetry compilation excises the vast majority of parameters while maintaining ground-state accuracy within the resolution of the reported benchmarks. In large TFIM systems, strong spatial constraints compress thousands of parameters down to tens, delivering substantial runtime accelerations. Our geometric diagnostics indicate that symmetry produces a more favorable target-aware geometry by concentrating the reachable state space around low-energy solutions while retaining broad target basins. Together, our results indicate that symmetry compilation concentrates the expressive power of NQS on states relevant to the target problem, thereby reducing model size and training cost without sacrificing accuracy.

papers.title: How to Test Bell Nonlocality for Gravity?
papers.abstract: We propose an experiment to test Bell nonlocality, a genuine nonclassicality, for the gravitational field. Two masses with embedded entangled spins (e.g., two diamonds with their NV-centre spins entangled) are placed well outside each other's light cones, ensuring a locality-loophole-free scenario. The spins are then coupled to the motion of their respective masses to generate spatial superpositions. Finally, local measurements are performed only on the gravitational fields of the two masses. If gravity is quantum, then the two entangled masses would entangle their gravitational fields, leading to correlations certifying Bell nonlocality of gravity. Trapped and ground-state cooled nano-objects with micron-sized spatial superposition are sufficient for this test. This goes beyond the recent proposals to test nonclassicality of gravity by providing, for the first time in the literature, a minimal tool to (i) create Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen (EPR) state of gravitational curvatures, (ii) witness entangled gravitational curvatures, (iii) rule out any local-realist description of gravity, and (iv) achieve a loophole-free test of gravity's nonclassicality in a fully device-independent way.

papers.title: Bona: Automatic Management of Dirty Ancilla Borrowing in Quantum Circuits
papers.abstract: The management of ancilla qubits has become a critical technique for reducing quantum circuit width. Dirty ancillas, which may be borrowed from any temporarily idle qubit regardless of their initial states, offer substantial flexibility for width optimization, but their use has so far required manual and error-prone handling. We formalize the dirty-qubit borrowing problem and establish a fundamental computational limit by proving its NP-hardness. To support practical optimization, we present \bona, the first scheduler for dirty-qubit borrowing, built on a novel depth-aware heuristic algorithm. We evaluate \bona~ across a variety of benchmarks, including practical quantum circuits and randomly arranged compositions of real circuit modules, and find that it reduces nearly 99\% of dirty ancillas on average with controlled depth overhead. In particular, for parallel quantum walk---an essential component of parallel Hamiltonian simulation---\bona~ matches the circuit width achieved by the clean-qubit schemes of \citeauthor{jiang2024recycling}~(\citeyear{jiang2024recycling}) and \citeauthor{quantinuum}~(\citeyear{quantinuum}), but attains significantly smaller circuit depth, providing concrete evidence that dirty ancillas offer unique optimization advantages in circuits with certain parallelism.

papers.title: Analytical Nuclear Gradients and Hessians on Quantum Hardware via Orbital-Optimized VQE with Error Mitigation
papers.abstract: Nuclear gradients and Hessians are fundamental quantities in computational chemistry, essential for a wide range of applications including geometry optimization, vibrational spectroscopy, and molecular property calculations. In this work, we present their analytical implementation on quantum hardware. The methodology is formulated within an active-space framework combining orbital optimization and linear-response theory. On the quantum-computing side, the approach employs the tiled unitary product state (tUPS) ansatz to directly evaluate the tensor elements required for solving the response equations. Moreover, the expectation values are corrected using an adapted confusion-matrix error-mitigation scheme in combination with post-selection criteria. The resulting workflow is assessed on molecular hydrogen and on water through the calculation of potential energy surfaces, nuclear gradients, Hessians, and vibrational frequencies, enabling the evaluation of both its capabilities and current limitations. The results demonstrate good performance for the hydrogen molecule, whereas the water molecule provides a more demanding test of quantum-hardware resources and highlights the trade-offs associated with error-mitigation strategies. The quantified analysis of the results identify the main sources of errors, suggesting improvement directions for more accurate quantum computer applications.

papers.title: Promise and Challenges of Distimation
papers.abstract: Estimating the quality of raw entangled states and distilling high-fidelity entanglement traditionally require two separate link-layer protocols in a quantum network stack, each consuming its own share of fragile entangled pairs. The recently introduced distimation concept merges these two protocols by directly extracting state estimation data from the classical syndromes generated during entanglement distillation. By removing the dedicated "test-then-distill'' stage, distimation lowers the number of raw entangled pairs required to operate the network, reduces latency, and streamlines the network control plane. The paradigm is especially attractive for near-term hardware platforms, where entanglement generation remains a severe bottleneck. Alongside these promises, distimation introduces new engineering challenges, ranging from accurate local-device modeling to protocols for tracking time-varying sources. This article surveys the core principles of distimation, quantifies expected gains for realistic architectures, and outlines a research roadmap toward making distimation a standard building block in future quantum networks.

papers.title: DA-CASE: reusable measurements for adaptive quantum subspaces
papers.abstract: Quantum subspace methods are often compared by basis dimension or energyerror, although their dominant experimental costs arise from different statepreparations, measurement settings, and shot allocations. We present theDyadic Adaptive Clifford-Algebra Subspace Eigensolver (DA-CASE), whose basisstates are virtual directions $A_i|ψ\rangle$ generated from one reference.Overlap, Hamiltonian, and observable matrices are reconstructed from onecached set of Pauli expectations on that reference. The method thereforetrades multiple prepared basis states for a potentially wide measurement bank.We make that trade explicit on a frozen eight-qubit H$_4$ Hamiltonian. Twogenerator resolutions reach the same nine-dimensional subspace and the sameenergy to machine precision, while the retained bank changes from 7371 to 2240Pauli words. A reference-conditioned symmetry test certifies the narrower spanwithout asserting that its individual Pauli words conserve the sector asabstract operators. Independently, a dyadic commuting hierarchy reduces thedeterminant bank from 913 qubit-wise-commuting settings to 64 fully commutingsettings, while exposing the added logical-CX cost. In a separate four-qubitfinite-shot diagnostic, covariance-aware allocation reduces theprojected-matrix variance target by 68.9%. Mode-wise overlap regularizationremoves the observed catastrophic energy estimates and lowers RMSE, butdoubles the median error relative to a fixed cutoff. These are small-instanceexact and Monte Carlo results, not a hardware demonstration, scaling result,or quantum advantage claim. The contribution is a single-referencemeasurement architecture and a resource ledger that keeps contexts, settings,shots, circuit depth, and post-selection retries in their proper units.

papers.title: Interaction between Rydberg Excitons in Cuprous Oxide Revealed through Resonant Second Harmonic Generation
papers.abstract: We report experimental and theoretical investigations of interacting excitons of the yellow series in cuprous oxide (Cu$_2$O) with principal quantum numbers up to by means of second harmonic generation (SHG). Using picosecond pulsed laser excitation up to 10 GW/cm$^2$ peak intensity we observe a pronounced change of the spectra with increasing pump laser intensity: an energetic shift to lower absolute energies and a spectral broadening. The absolute intensities of the spectral lines scale for low powers with the square of the pump power, but saturates at higher powers. At still higher powers the SHG intensity is actually reduced. To explain these results quantitively, we developed a semi-classical theory of resonant SHG where the process of SHG is fully coherent. The excitons are assumed to be bosons interacting by a distance dependent potential giving rise to both the changes in spectral line shape and the saturation by a $\it{Rydberg}$ blockade. The concomitant measurement of two-photon absorption allows to derive quantitative values for the exciton-exciton interaction. While the results agree in order of magnitude with those calculated by state-of-the art atomic-like van der Waals interaction theory, the scaling with principle quantum number is quite different. As a possible screening by an electron-hole plasma created by three-photon absorption into blue and violet band states could be ruled out, our results point toward fundamental differences between excitons and atoms.

papers.title: A Resource-Efficient Quantum Framework for Graph Coloring and Chromatic Number Estimation
papers.abstract: Many industrial optimization tasks can be modeled as graph coloring, where adjacent vertices must have different colors. This NP-hard problem is challenging for large graphs. We present a quantum encoding requiring qubits that scale logarithmically with the number of colors and linearly with vertices. Using adiabatic evolution with a novel mixer Hamiltonian and vertex terms, we compute the chromatic number and demonstrate robustness by solving constrained truck loading problems.

papers.title: Point-gap topology in amorphous non-Hermitian quantum systems
papers.abstract: Recent studies have revealed that not only does the correspondence between spectral winding numbers and skin modes break down in non-Hermitian systems, but the energy spectrum itself is highly sensitive to generic perturbations, system size, and boundary conditions. In amorphous non-Hermitian systems, where the positions of lattice sites are uncertain, the spectral instability becomes even more severe, making it difficult to identify stable topological edge states from the eigenvalue spectrum alone. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a correspondence between stable zero-mode singular states and mid-gap states of the energy spectrum in the thermodynamic limit. Because the singular value spectrum is highly robust against small perturbations and variation in size, topological edge states can be reliably probed via singular values even in finite-sized systems. Based on the singular-value decomposition of the Hamiltonian, we construct a topological invariant in real space to characterize the associated topologically protected edge states. Our approach provides a general strategy for exploring point-gap topology in real space and redefine the non-Hermitian skin effect from a new perspective.

papers.title: What solvable models reveal about Born-Oppenheimer, Born-Huang, and exact factorization
papers.abstract: The Born-Oppenheimer (BO) and single-surface Born-Huang (BH) approximations replace the full molecular problem by nuclear motion associated with one clamped electronic state, whereas the full BH expansion and exact factorization (EF) are exact representations. We use two analytically transparent models to identify what controls one-surface error. For Fernández's bilinearly coupled oscillators, the Brattsev ground-state bracket was already known; we derive closed-form differences proving strictness for every positive nuclear mass and nonzero stable coupling. Using Hunter's conditional-amplitude construction, we place the closed-form ground-state EF potential alongside BO and single-surface BH. Exact excited-state calculations show that the bracket does not extend through the spectrum. The diagonal BH correction is the quantum-metric coefficient of the retained electronic state divided by twice the nuclear mass. Fernández's sixth-order expansion shows that the next omitted correction contains the same derivative couplings, an additional inverse electronic-energy separation, and a factor depending on the nuclear state. We therefore add a two-state model with a position-dependent gap. Decreasing its minimum separation makes the metric higher and narrower while leaving the total Fubini-Study length equal to pi/2. The exact EF, BO, and BH potentials can differ visibly even when their nuclear ground-state amplitudes are nearly identical. The two models show that one-surface accuracy depends on nuclear mass, electronic-state variation, energy separation from omitted states, and the nuclear wavefunction.

papers.title: Dissipation-engineered dual-charger quantum batteries
papers.abstract: Suppressing coherent energy backflow while maintaining extractable energy in a stable nonequilibrium state remains a central challenge for quantum energy storage. Here, we introduce a reservoir-engineered dual-charger quantum battery architecture, in which nonequilibrium dissipation is exploited as a control resource to stabilize useful stored energy. A hot-reservoir-coupled driver supplies excitations, while a cold-reservoir-coupled cache biases the resonant three-body transition toward charging and suppresses the dressed-state coherences responsible for energy backflow. This mechanism establishes a population-inverted steady state with finite ergotropy and converts reversible charger--battery exchange into persistent energy storage. For uniformly spaced multilevel batteries, we show that the stored energy and ergotropy scale approximately linearly with the number of accessible levels, while the stored-energy utilization approaches unity. The accompanying stationary heat current provides a thermodynamic signature of the charging regime. Our results demonstrate dissipation engineering as a strategy for achieving stable and scalable quantum energy storage beyond transient coherent charging protocols.

papers.title: Quantum discord of Ganssian states in an expanding universe
papers.abstract: We investigate the redistribution of continuous-variable quantum discord within the framework of an expanding universe. We find that quantum discord exhibits stronger sensitivity to the spacetime expansion rate than to the expansion volume. As both the expansion rate and expansion volume increase, the initial quantum discord shared by the two bosonic modes decays, while quantum discord is induced in additional mode pairs by the underlying spacetime expansion, signaling a global redistribution of quantum correlations across the system. Specifically, the induced discord is largest for cross-observer bosonic-antibosonic pairs, followed by same-observer bosonic-antibosonic pairs, and smallest for the pair of antibosonic modes. Furthermore, our quantum discord analysis demonstrates that particles with lower momentum and optimal mass serve as more favorable candidates for extracting information about the expanding universe. This work substantially enriches the theoretical framework of quantum discord in expanding spacetimes, and provides new perspectives as well as a solid theoretical foundation for further investigations.

papers.title: Levitated Milligram-scale Ferromagnetic Magnetometer at Room Temperature
papers.abstract: Levitated mechanical oscillators are emerging ultrasensitive sensors with tremendous potential in both applied and fundamental physics. Levitated ferromagnets, with internal spin noises rapidly averaged, promise ultrahigh magnetic sensitivity. Here, we demonstrate a milligram-scale diamagnetically levitated ferromagnet system operating at room temperature. Through optimized geometry and multi-channel dissipation control, we achieve a magnetic sensitivity of 23~fT$/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$ at frequency of 100-Hz level. We anticipate that a ferromagnetic magnetometer with subfemtotesla sensitivity is within reach, after modest technical improvements. This platform establishes a high-performance magnetometer for biomagnetic field detection and beyond-standard-model force searches.

papers.title: Quantum-Device Simulation of Optical Decoherence of Hole-Spin Qubits in Self-Assembled Quantum Dots
papers.abstract: Spin-photon interfaces are essential for communications between distant spin qubits in quantum technologies, but the interband optical excitation can also damp electrically driven hole-spin Rabi oscillations in semiconductor self-assembled quantum dots (SAQDs). We report a device-level modeling workflow that integrates realistic SAQD geometry and multiband electronic-structure analysis with models of electrically driven spin control, interband optical transitions, and open-system dynamics. This workflow enables device-level estimation of Rabi-oscillation damping arising from repeated interband absorption-emission cycles. As an example, for a gated GaAs SAQD subjected to a uniform magnetic field $B_0$ along the growth direction of the SAQD, we predict the Rabi frequency of the hole spin qubit and its damping under external illumination. At $B_0=2$ T, the calculations yield a hole-spin Rabi frequency of 37.3 MHz. When the electrically driven SAQD is illuminated by a broadband LED centered at a wavelength of 790 nm, increasing the optical power from 0.3 to 1.5 mW shortens the Rabi-oscillation decay time from 90.3 to 17.5 ns. Increasing the SAQD height reduces the electron-hole overlap and thus the emission rate, but the resulting redshift moves the interband transitions into stronger spectral overlap with the LED spectrum, thereby increasing the rate of repeated absorption-emission cycles and enhancing photon-induced Rabi-oscillation damping. The results show that geometry, spin-control conditions, and illumination spectrum should be co-optimized in semiconductor spin-photon devices.

papers.title: Effect of Strong Field Space-time Features on Vacuum Pair
papers.abstract: The relativistic dynamics of bound states across inertial reference frames are investigated using the computational quantum field theory (CQFT). The results reveal that the spatiotemporal properties of bound states within a given potential well are strictly frame-dependent. Crucially, this spatiotemporal modulation of the external field enables a reduction in the laser intensity threshold required for vacuum electron-positron pair creation. Analytical and numerical calculations demonstrate that this threshold reduction originates from the Lorentz transformation of the four-momentum, which reshapes the vacuum excitation pathways in phase space. By developing CQFT, we establish a comprehensive framework in which relativistic effects intrinsically govern the quantum vacuum decay process

papers.title: The Input Problem: A Permanent Bottleneck for Quantum Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Quantum algorithms are conventionally presented with their input state supplied for free. When the input is classical data, this convention conceals a cost that is frequently larger than the algorithm it precedes. We review what the three standard encodings, such as basis encoding, amplitude encoding, and Grover--Rudolph distribution loading, actually cost once transpiled to a hardware gate set, and argue that the resulting $Θ(N)$ bound is a counting theorem rather than an engineering limitation that improved hardware will remove. Measured gate counts for a representative loading task are reported: an optimal library implementation requires $247$ CNOT gates at $n=8$ qubits and doubles with each additional qubit, while the classical preprocessing that produces the rotation angles requires reading the entire input vector. We show how this cost eliminates the quadratic advantage of quantum amplitude estimation for Monte Carlo integration, and argue that the same accounting constrains quantum machine learning more broadly: the strong input models that make quantum algorithms fast on classical data also enable classical dequantization, and quantum kernel methods carry a $Θ(M^2)$ state-preparation cost for the Gram matrix that does not amortize. We explain that the efficiently preparable states, device-generated distributions, variationally learned loading, and amortized preparation are required to get advantage from quantum machine learning and close with a checklist for evaluating input-dependent advantage claims. Executable notebooks reproducing every construction and measurement discussed here are available.

papers.title: Optimal strategies for shadow tomography with limited resources
papers.abstract: Shadow tomography addresses the task of efficiently predicting many expectation values of an unknown quantum state from randomized measurements on comparatively few copies. Existing analyses promise large scaling advantages, but the optimal strategies realizing these guarantees are not always known, and the required measurements are potentially challenging to implement on current hardware. We address this gap for Pauli observables by computing optimal sample-complexity parameters and constructing optimal measurement strategies under realistic resource constraints. We focus on memoryless protocols, where each copy is measured only once, and on measurements with bounded interaction range. Our approach reduces the problem to the analysis of graph parameters of the frustration graph encoding the Pauli anticommutation relations. We provide efficient numerical methods for the general case and analytically prove that Clifford measurements are optimal in many situations. This includes all perfect graphs, all single-qubit, all two-qubit measurement scenarios, and more. Applied to Hamiltonian energy estimation, our framework yields constructive strategies and improved variance bounds for molecular benchmarks.

papers.title: Deep Holes in the Clifford Hierarchy
papers.abstract: We determine the covering radius of the topological closure of the single-qubit Clifford hierarchy in $\SU(2)\cong S^3$. This closure is a union of $18$ great circles --- the Clifford--Pauli circles --- and we prove that its covering radius is $\arccos\sqrt{5/6}$. The extremal points, which we call \emph{deep holes}, form a single orbit of size $192$ under left and right multiplication by Clifford gates, and are described in closed form. Equivalently, the minimum over one-qubit unitaries of the all-level Clifford fidelity is $5/6$. The proof rests on two structures attached to the configuration of $18$ planes in $\R^4$: their centered rank-two projectors form an orthonormal basis of the irreducible $\SO(4)$-module $\Sym_0(4)$, and the projection profile of a unit quaternion is exactly its image under the double cover $\SU(2)\to\SO(3)$. These reduce the covering problem to a minimax statement for the $\ell^\infty$-norm on $\SO(3)$ which we solve exactly, classifying its equality cases.

papers.title: Fisher-Information Geometry Linking Schrodinger Dynamics, Bipartite Correlations, and Decoherence
papers.abstract: Fisher information appears in quantum theory in two mathematically distinct settings: as a classical probability functional in variational reconstructions of Schrodinger dynamics and as the quantum Fisher metric of parameterized density operators. Here we examine how far these roles can be connected without identifying the two objects. Starting from a Hamilton-Jacobi ensemble action, we recover the Fisher term that generates the quantum potential and isolate its contribution to the kinetic-energy expectation. We then analyze the quantum Fisher information matrix (QFIM) of bipartite states. For any pure two-qubit state, the optimized magnitude of the off-diagonal QFIM element for normalized local generators equals the concurrence, while a collective phase generator yields FQ = 4 C^2. Extending the optimized pure-state quantity by a convex roof gives an exact identity with Wootters concurrence for arbitrary mixed two-qubit states. This differs from evaluating the QFIM directly on a mixed density operator: for Werner states the raw optimized cross-QFIM is 2 p^2/(1 + p) and remains nonzero inside the separable region. The gap between the raw and convex-roof quantities therefore isolates, for this family, correlation geometry not captured by entanglement. Finally, in a two-path interferometer with a which-way marker, the optimal phase Fisher information available from local output statistics is I_phi^opt = V^2. These results place probability-gradient energy, bipartite correlation geometry, entanglement, and decoherence-induced loss of local phase sensitivity in a common mathematical setting while preserving the distinctions between classical Fisher information, QFIM geometry, Bell nonlocality, and global phase quantization.

papers.title: Entanglement and non-local magic in a non-unitarily deformed non-Hermitian bipartite system
papers.abstract: Non-Hermitian degeneracies are usually discussed through spectral coalescence, whereas entanglement is a property of eigenvectors and need not be fixed by the eigenvalues alone. We formulate a compact bipartite model that separates these two notions. A Hermitian operator with a degenerate eigenspace is transformed by an invertible non-unitary similarity map. The resulting Hamiltonian is non-Hermitian and retains a non-defective degeneracy at every finite value of the non-Hermiticity parameter. For an exactly solvable two-qubit realization, the right eigenstates evolve continuously from product states to maximally entangled states although the spectrum is unchanged. We distinguish the positive right-state reduced density matrix from the generally non-positive biorthogonal reduction, for which entropy may become complex. The same two-qubit solution gives a closed partial-transpose negativity and a Schmidt-gauged non-local magic. Entanglement grows monotonically with the non-Hermiticity parameter, whereas the non-local magic vanishes for both the product and maximally entangled limits and is largest at an intermediate coupling. In larger bipartite spaces, the Page entropy and Haar-averaged purity provide reference values for eigenstate typicality. These diagnostics separate non-defective degeneracy, exceptional-point sensitivity, Haar-typical entanglement, and non-stabilizer correlations without relying on a proliferation of basis-dependent spectral quantities.

papers.title: Local Complex Dependence and Separability in Madelung Hydrodynamics
papers.abstract: For a many-particle pure state in a fixed position representation, we consider the mixed cross-particle derivatives of the logarithm of the wave function. Their real part is one half of the Holland-Wang local dependence function of the configuration density, while their imaginary part is the cross-Jacobian of the Madelung velocity field. On a node-free product region, vanishing of all cross blocks throughout the region is equivalent to local multiplicative separability. Under Schrodinger evolution with a real scalar potential, the initial growth of a cross block from a separable state is sourced by the corresponding mixed Hessian of the potential and is purely imaginary to first order in time. The construction is a local separability and dependence diagnostic, rather than a basis-independent entanglement measure.

papers.title: Randomness Certification and Trade-offs in the Prepare-and-Broadcast Scenario
papers.abstract: We investigate the prepare-and-broadcast scenario, a multipartite extension of dimension-constrained prepare-and-measure experiments in which a quantum system is distributed to multiple receivers.
